Neonatal Gummy sharks (Mustelus antarcticus) emerge from their mothers after a prolonged gestation period of approximately 11 to 12 months. At birth, the pups measure roughly 32.5 cm [Lb = roughly 32.5 cm] in total length, a dimension that places them among the smaller-bodied neonates of the triakid sharks. Field surveys conducted in southeastern Australian waters consistently report a range of 30 to 35 cm for newborn individuals (30-35 cm) [Lb = 30-35 cm], with the mean value aligning well with laboratory-based observations. This size at birth reflects a substantial maternal investment in yolk-dependent embryonic development, which occurs entirely within the uterus. The age at birth, or the duration from fertilisation to parturition, spans approximately 350 days [ab = approximately 350 days] when measured at a stable water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This extended gestation is typical of many temperate elasmobranchs and is thought to be linked to the relatively cool thermal regime of their continental-shelf habitat, which slows metabolic processes during embryogenesis. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Mustelus mustelus suggest that the Gummy shark's gestation period is broadly consistent with that of other members of the genus inhabiting similar latitudes.

Furthermore, reproductive frequency in this species is low; females generally produce a single litter every two years [F_R_i = single litter every two years], a pattern observed consistently in long-term tagging studies at an ambient temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This biennial reproductive cycle, combined with the modest litter sizes, yields a relatively low maximum reproductive rate of approximately 0.026 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.026 pups per day] at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The combination of a 1 to 38 pup range per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 38 pup range per litter] and a single litter every two years [F_R_i = single litter every two years] indicates a conservative life-history strategy that is sensitive to overfishing pressure. The slow pace of reproduction is further underscored by the fact that females invest substantial energy in each litter, as evidenced by the relatively large size of the pups at birth.

The ultimate total length attained by Gummy sharks has been documented through extensive commercial fishery landings and independent scientific surveys. The largest verified specimen of Mustelus antarcticus measured 175 cm [Li = 175 cm] in total length, a value that represents the upper extreme of what this species can achieve. However, more commonly encountered adults rarely exceed 157 cm [Li = 157 cm] in total length, suggesting that the 175 cm record is exceptional and may be associated with particularly favourable feeding conditions or advanced age. These asymptotic sizes place the Gummy shark among the medium-bodied members of the Triakidae family. The difference between the maximum recorded length and the more typical maximum reflects the natural variation inherent in wild populations, where resource availability and environmental conditions modulate somatic growth trajectories. Growth curves derived from vertebral banding patterns indicate that individuals continue to increase in length throughout much of their lifespan, albeit at a decreasing rate after the onset of sexual maturation. This deceleration is common among elasmobranchs and is linked to the energetic demands of reproduction.

Puberty in the Gummy shark, marking the onset of reproductive capability, is attained at a total length of approximately 119.5 cm [Lp = approximately 119.5 cm]. Field studies across the species' range, however, reveal considerable geographic variation, with the age at maturity corresponding to a length range of 85 to 130 cm (85-130 cm) [Lp = 85-130 cm], depending on local growth rates and resource availability. At the point of sexual maturation, the corresponding wet body mass is considerable; individuals at puberty weigh approximately 7,500 grams [Wwp = approximately 7,500 grams], a figure derived from length–weight relationships established for the species. For fully grown adults that have reached their ultimate dimensions, the maximum wet weight recorded is around 24,700 grams [Wwi = around 24,700 grams], reflecting the substantial additional somatic growth that continues well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. This body mass at puberty underscores the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive effort can commence, a pattern typical of slow-growing, long-lived marine predators. The disparity between the two mass estimates highlights the complex allometric relationships in this species.

Lifespan estimates for Mustelus antarcticus have been derived from both vertebral ageing techniques and mark-recapture studies conducted in southern Australian waters. The maximum documented lifespan in the wild is approximately 45 years [am = approximately 45 years], as reported in FishBase and corroborated by several independent studies at a mean water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The relatively cool thermal environment of its continental-shelf habitat, typically around 16 °C, likely contributes to this extended lifespan by slowing physiological ageing processes.
